When the admission letter finally arrived, the paper itself was not thick.
But everyone in the family knew its weight was not in the paper.
In 1990, Zhang Yuansheng was admitted to a university undergraduate program.

Years later, it would take only one line on a résumé: admitted to university, 1990. At the time, however, it meant that a child from an ordinary family had, for the first time, used his own results to push his life a little farther outward.

His father, as usual, did not show his happiness dramatically. His mother repeated the news to relatives and close friends. Neighbours offered congratulations, and the atmosphere at home felt different from ordinary days.
Yuansheng himself found it hard to say exactly what he felt.

There was excitement, of course. There was also that careless confidence particular to youth: if the hardest hurdle had been cleared, university would probably be much freer than high school. As for what he would do after graduation or where he would go, there was no need to know yet.
Starting university meant leaving home in a real sense for the second time.
This time the whole family was not moving with him.
The luggage was his, and so was the road. His parents could accompany him part of the way, but they could not move into the new life with him.

The first thing he noticed when he saw the university campus was how many people there were. Young people from different places had been gathered into the same campus, each bringing an accent, habits, and a past. Some spoke as if they had already seen much of the world. Others, like him, were encountering many things for the first time.
The dormitory was the university’s first real lesson.

Several people lived in limited space. Beds, desks, hot water, laundry, and conversations that continued long after lights-out made strangers familiar faster than classrooms did. Young people from very different families were living away from their parents for the first time, and many habits had nowhere to hide.
Yuansheng discovered that freedom really had arrived.

But freedom was not the imagined pleasure of “no one controls me.” It was more like having many decisions once made by parents and teachers suddenly thrown into his own hands: when to sleep, whether to study tonight, how to spend money, what to do after falling behind in a course, which friends to keep close.
When no one checks every day, it becomes easier to see where a person will eventually lead himself.
Of course, there were books to study at university.

But what a young person truly learns often extends far beyond the timetable: measuring himself for the first time in a larger crowd, discovering that things others do well may be difficult for him, encountering ideas unlike those at home, and seriously imagining words such as work and marriage that once belonged only to adults.
China was changing quickly in those years too.

Young people on campus could feel an acceleration. People talked about markets, the south, and opportunity. An “iron rice bowl” still held attraction, but the question of what came next no longer felt as fixed as it had for the previous generation.
Yuansheng did not suddenly become someone who chased every opportunity.

A steady part of his character remained strong. Rather than imagine the future as a gamble, he preferred to do the work in front of him well. Yet the curiosity about “outside” that had grown during his oilfield years never disappeared either.
He wondered how far a person could travel in one lifetime.

Back then, “far” still meant geography: a larger city, a better job, a place unlike the one he knew. No one would have imagined that a little more than a decade later he would pack his life into luggage and fly to Canada.
During his university years, he gradually changed from a student into a young man preparing to enter society.

The childishness in his face faded. Conversations began to include salary, work units, job assignments, and positions. Graduation was no longer a distant ceremony. It came closer and forced everyone to answer a practical question: where next?
For Zhang Yuansheng, the answer would eventually lead back to the oilfield.
It seemed almost like a circle.
At twelve, the oilfield had carried him out of Zhaojiadian Village. After university, he would return to that vast system, this time as an employee in his own right.
But a circle is not the same as standing still.
The young man returning from university was no longer the boy who had left home to study.
The door opened by that admission letter in 1990 did not send him directly into a completely unfamiliar life.
It first taught him something simpler: some doors in life could be opened by his own hand.
